newsitem.title: USA: American talks in critical phase as strike looms.
newsitem.headline: American talks in critical phase as strike looms.

text.p: American Airlines and its pilots made slow progress Friday in talks to avert a strike that would ground the nation's second-largest carrier and disrupt the holiday plans of thousands of travelers.

But there was no certainty agreement would be reached before a midnight strike deadline as air travelers around the country braced for cancelled flights and long delays over the busy Presidents Day weekend.

"We're negotiating very hard. Progress is coming but it's coming slowly, but it's part of the give and take of negotiations," American spokesman Chris Chiames said during a brief break in talks. "Clearly the next few hours are going to be critical to whether we're going to get a deal."
James Sovic, president of the Allied Pilots Association, described the talks as "slow and difficult."
The negotiations had reached a "critical" phase by late afternoon, said Kenneth Hipp, chairman of the National Mediation Board, which is overseeing the bargaining.

The pilots have set a midnight (0500 GMT Saturday) deadline for an agreement to avert a strike that would shut down the airline, which carries 20 percent of the nation's air travelers, and could cost the economy $200 million a day.

Fort Worth, Texas-based American has 2,200 flights that carry about 200,000 passengers a day. It has cancelled most of its international flights and a few domestic flights in anticipation of a strike.

With the hours ticking away, pressure grew on President Bill Clinton to act to avert a damaging blow to the economy. Hipp tried to dispel speculation that Clinton would use his powers to declare an emergency and prevent a strike.
"I have no reason to believe that a presidential emergency board has been arranged," Hipp told reporters and then repeated the statement.
Clinton could create a special emergency board to forge a compromise, which would prevent a work stoppage for 60 days while the deal was drawn up and considered by both sides.
The White House refused to discuss possible presidential intervention in the dispute and Clinton again urged the airline and the union to work out a solution.
"They need to go back to work. They have a few more hours of work to do," Clinton said, looking at his watch, after a reporter asked if he would intervene to avert a strike.

Travel agents said any strike would batter the tourist industry in the Caribbean, which is in its peak winter holiday season, and could cause havoc as well at major airports in Chicago, Miami, New York and Los Angeles and other cities.
Some airports were jammed on Friday as passengers scrambled to rearrange their plans.
The key issues in the talks are pay for pilots flying big jets and whether members of the Allied Pilots Association should fly smaller jets for American's commuter carrier, American Eagle.
American has said it needs to fly the new, small jets with lower-paid pilots from another union if it is to compete with other major carriers offering low-cost commuter flights.

Brian Mayhew, the pilots' chief negotiator, said on Thursday that the pilots had offered a new proposal on pay -- presumably less than the 11.5 percent pay increase over four years sought earlier -- but gave no details. The latest offer from American was a 6 percent raise over four years.
The stock of AMR Corp., American's parent company, fell $1.25 to $81.875 on the New York Stock Exchange.
